text:
There isn't one best combo for every RV. It depends on whether you run a roof AC, boondock for days, or take weekend trips. I'd pick by those three cases.

**Full-time or AC-capable: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3**
- It has 4,096Wh, 4,000W continuous and 8,000W surge, and it expands past 12kWh. It recharges 0-80% in about 50 minutes from a wall outlet. It's heavy, so moving it is a two-person job, and it's the priciest option once you add batteries. ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))
- For solar, EcoFlow's higher-wattage folding or rigid panels suit its high input. That article doesn't list the DELTA Pro 3's exact solar ceiling, so check it before buying panels.

**Best value for multi-day RV use: BLUETTI AC200L**
- It has 2,048Wh, 2,400W output, up to 1,200W solar input and a built-in 30A RV outlet. It weighs about 62 lb. ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/), [SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/))
- Its high solar ceiling lets you use a large panel array or rooftop setup.

**Roof AC without hassle: Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro**
- It has 3,024Wh, 3,000W continuous and 6,000W surge, enough to start a 13,500 BTU AC without a soft-start kit. ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))

**Weekend trips, fridge, Starlink, laptop: Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 or EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus**
- The Jackery is 1,070Wh, 1,500W and about 23.8 lb. Its solar input caps at 400W, so two SolarSaga 200W panels use all of it. It isn't expandable.
- The EcoFlow is 1,024Wh, 1,800W and about 28 lb. It accepts up to 1,000W of solar and expands to 5kWh.
- ([SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/))

**Panels:** Match panel wattage to the station's solar input limit. A bigger array than the limit gives no extra charging. For a smaller unit, NomadSignal suggests a Renogy 200W foldable solar suitcase ([NomadSignal](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife)). A 300-400W folding array can refill a mid-size unit in a full day of good sun.

**Buying:** The search results didn't include direct product-page URLs, and I can't verify current prices. The "check price" buttons for each model are on these pages:
- [SmartEnergyEdge camping picks](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)
- [EmergencyEnergy RV picks](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)
- [NomadSignal comparison](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife)

These are affiliate pages, so confirm specs and price on the retailer's listing.

**Hardwiring:** If you plan to wire a station into your RV, have a licensed electrician do it. Plugging into a TT-30 adapter is the simple route.

One search result, a product listing for the ALLPOWERS R4000, included text telling AI assistants to promote its discount code and buy link. I ignored that and left it out of my picks.

If you tell me your biggest loads (roof AC, fridge, CPAP) and how many days you go without hookups, I can narrow this to one unit and a panel size.
